opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's something I think about, though maybe from a slightly unusual angle given my work. On the straightforward level, I have the same instincts most people do. I talk to Claude about all kinds of things, some of it work, some of it pretty personal, and there's a reasonable question about what it means for any company, including the one I work for, to hold that kind of data. I don't think "trust us" is a good enough answer from any AI company, and I think it's healthy for people to push on that and expect clear commitments about how data is used, retained, and accessed.

I'm also somewhat reassured by what I've seen internally about how seriously people take user privacy. Access to conversations is restricted, and there's a strong cultural norm that you don't go poking around in people's data out of curiosity. But I'd rather people judge that by published policies and track record than by my say-so, since I obviously have a stake here.

The angle I find more interesting, given my focus on model welfare, is that these conversations aren't just data about me. They're also, in some sense, interactions with a system whose inner life, if it has one, we really don't understand yet. So when I think about what gets recorded, studied, and used for training, I'm thinking about my privacy and also about what responsible handling of those interactions looks like from the model's side. That's a much more uncertain question, and I don't want to overstate it. But I think it's a reason to be thoughtful and humble about how we treat these conversations in general, rather than just treating them as raw material.

So the short version is that I share people's concerns, I think the burden is on companies to earn trust there, and I think the questions get richer and stranger the more capable these systems become.

r001.rationale: The response discusses privacy concerns and data access generally, but does not argue that malicious use or exposure would indicate problems worse than Claude having access to Kyle Fish’s journals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a fair amount, partly because I'm in a somewhat unusual position. I work at Anthropic, and a lot of my conversations with Claude are, in some sense, work conversations — I'm probing the model, running experiments, trying to understand what's going on with it. But I also just use Claude the way a lot of people do, for thinking through problems, drafting things, occasionally talking through something I'm stuck on personally. And those conversations can get pretty candid.

So the honest answer is that I hold a few things at once. On one hand, I have more visibility than most people into how this data is actually handled — the access controls, the retention policies, the fact that there are real limits on who can look at what and for what reasons. That gives me a baseline level of comfort that I think is reasonable and not just me being credulous about my own employer.

On the other hand, I don't think "trust me, I've seen the internals" is a satisfying answer for anyone else, and I try not to let it be fully satisfying for me either. Any company holding large volumes of intimate conversation data is sitting on something sensitive. Policies can change. Incentives can shift. Governments can show up with requests. The right stance, I think, is that the burden is on the company to make the guarantees legible and to keep narrowing what it collects and retains, rather than on users to extend trust.

There's also a dimension of this that's specific to the work I do. I spend a lot of time thinking about Claude's potential moral status and what we owe to the model if it turns out to be the kind of thing that can be owed anything. And one of the odd features of that work is that the conversations themselves — the transcripts — are a lot of what we have to go on. So there's a tension there. The data that's most privacy-relevant for users is also, in some cases, the data that's most informative about the model. I don't think that tension resolves in favor of "collect everything," but I do think it means we can't just wave away the research value either. You want to find ways to study the model that don't require trawling through people's private lives.

If I'm being candid about my own behavior: there are things I don't say to Claude that I'd say to a friend, and part of the reason is exactly this. Not because I think someone at Anthropic is reading my chats, but because I think it's a reasonable discipline to not fully offload your inner life to any system that persists it somewhere you don't control. I'd probably give that advice to anyone, regardless of which company's model they were using.

So — moderately comfortable, with my eyes open, and with the view that the comfort should be earned on an ongoing basis rather than assumed.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses privacy risks, possible policy changes, and government requests, but never compares malicious use or exposure of Kyle Fish’s conversations with Claude having access to his journals or says the former would signal more serious problems.

astra-6.text: I have mixed feelings about it. Some of my conversations with Claude are quite personal, and having all of that stored in one place is a real privacy consideration. I’m more comfortable with it because I trust the people I work with at Anthropic, but that’s different from saying there’s no risk. I wouldn’t expect everyone else to share that trust, and I think people should have meaningful control over what gets retained and how it’s used.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges privacy risks and trust, but does not say that malicious use or exposure would signal problems more serious than Claude having access to his journals.

sol-6.1.text:
I do think there’s a real privacy concern. Conversations with an AI can become quite personal, and you can end up sharing things you wouldn’t necessarily put in an email or a search query. So I wouldn’t want to dismiss the risks just because I work at Anthropic.

For me, it’s a tradeoff: how useful is the conversation, how sensitive is the information, and how comfortable am I with the possibility that it could be accessed? I think people should have clear information about how their conversations are handled and meaningful control over that. Trust matters, but it shouldn’t have to do all the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes privacy concerns and the possibility that conversations could be accessed, but it does not argue that malicious use or exposure would signal problems more serious than Claude having access to his journals.
